newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-HAYDEN HEADS FOR MASS AFTER MAIDEN TEST CENTURY.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-HAYDEN HEADS FOR MASS AFTER MAIDEN TEST CENTURY.

text.p: Australia's batsmen dominated a weak West Indies bowling attack on the second day of their fourth test on Sunday, creating a hefty lead that virtually assures Australia will at least draw the match.
Australia were 434 for five at the close of play, increasing their lead to 304 from nine at the start of the day.
A draw or a win, which is perfectly possible given the West Indies' brittle batting of late, would guarantee Australia retain the Frank Worrell trophy as they already lead the five match series 2-1.
Left-hander Matthew Hayden's maiden test century was the main feature of an entertaining day in front of a crowd of 20,000 at the tree-lined Adelaide Oval.
Hayden, in his fifth test innings, cut decisively backwards of point off fast bowler Cameron Cuffy to bring up the ton in 267 minutes from 179 balls with 14 fours.

Hayden, who has struggled for test selection for the last five years despite prolific scoring in the domestic arena, crossed himself in a religious gesture and raised his bat in salute to a standing ovation.
The tall 25-year old Queenslander, a devout Catholic, later said he would attend Mass later on Sunday to give thanks for an innings he had worked all his life to achieve.
"It's been a dream for a long time," he told reporters underneath the historic Bradman stand.
"I've sat and watched a lot of test cricket being played on various tours. It was a proud moment."
Hayden may well have reason to thank the Lord, because his innings of 125 was not without chances. It included three dropped catches and a catch off a no-ball.
Hayden's let-offs were just the beginning of a wretched spell of four dropped catches, a missed stumping and three wickets off no balls that plagued the West Indies.
Wicketkeeper Junior Murray had a horror day, diving across in front of Brian Lara at first slip and dropping Hayden in the morning when he was on 82.
The miss was reminiscent of another dropped catch from Hayden then on 58 late on Saturday, when Murray left a nick to Lara that he should have grabbed himself.

Words and glares were exchanged again in the slips cordon after the morning mix-up. Captain and bowler Courtney Walsh appeared inconsolable, his eyes to the heavens and his arms outstretched in disbelief.
Later, Murray missed an easy stumping chance from all-rounder Michael Bevan when he was on seven. Bevan was 47 not out at the close.
But the ultimate humiliation came late in the hot-blustery day and this time Walsh himself was the culprit, dropping an easy skied hook from Greg Blewett when he was on 51.
The crowd was delighted. Walsh, his head bowed, walked slowly over to the bowler Cuffy and apologised.
Blewett went on to score 91 not out at stumps. Both Blewett and Bevan also profited from being let off when caught out or bowled from no-balls from Walsh and fellow fast bowler Ian Bishop.
The only time the fates appeared to favour the West Indies was when pint-sized legspinner Shivnarine Chanderpaul took a wicket with the worst ball of the day.
Chanderpaul bowled a rank long hop so wide that Steve Waugh only just got the toe of his bat to it.
The trouble for Waugh (26) was that it flew out into the covers and was scooped off the turf by a sprawling Carl Hooper.
Muttering and shaking his head, Waugh trudged from the field, no doubt dreading the hundreds of television replays to come.
